I wanted it to slide, and not just the sidebar on its own. I wanted the story river to move in sync with it, as one motion, so the page feels like it is opening and closing rather than snapping between two states. That turned out to be the whole project. ## Why Vanilla jumps This was the interesting part to learn. Vanilla doesn’t change the layout by animating anything. It swaps CSS rules. The `if-no-sidebar` and `if-fluid-fixed` macros wrap CSS text inside a reveal widget, so toggling `$:/state/sidebar` rewrites the stylesheet itself. A rewritten stylesheet lands in a single frame. There is no “before” value for the browser to animate from. So it jumps. It isn’t a bug, it’s just what that approach does. ## What Vanilla Notebook does instead Every rule is written once, unconditionally. Nothing is swapped. State arrives as a class on the page container, using the core’s existing `$:/tags/ClassFilters/PageTemplate` hook, and that class sets a single number: `@property --nb-open { syntax: ""; inherits: true; initial-value: 1; } ` `--nb-open` goes from 1 to 0, and because it’s registered with a real `` type, the browser can interpolate it. The sidebar’s position and the story river’s width are both written in terms of that one number, so they can’t drift apart. One value, one transition, and everything moves together. It works in both layout modes and in both text directions. One honest note, because I think it matters: in fixed-fluid the river keeps its width, so nothing reflows and the whole thing is genuinely composited. In fluid-fixed the river has to grow into the freed space, and that is layout work by definition. It is smooth and it doesn’t jump, but I’m not going to call it GPU accelerated, because it isn’t. ## How it was made I built it with Hallmark, a design skill for AI coding assistants: github.com ### GitHub - Nutlope/hallmark: Anti-AI-slop design skill for Claude Code, Cursor,... Anti-AI-slop design skill for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. The part that mattered most here is that Hallmark starts by reading what already exists rather than generating over the top of it. So Vanilla’s stylesheet was read end to end first. Not to copy it, but to learn which class names TiddlyWiki actually emits and what each one has to do. Vanilla is around 3,700 lines and carries a lot of hard-won knowledge about the core’s markup. Notebook is a standalone theme. It doesn’t depend on Vanilla and inherits no rule from it. But it was written by someone who had read Vanilla carefully, and quite a few of its rules exist only because Vanilla taught me they were needed. ## What it looks like Cream paper, warm ink, and a red margin rule down each tiddler, like a school notebook. Three type roles instead of the usual two: a serif for reading, a sans for the interface, a mono for code and file paths. The editor is ruled like paper, with the lines locked to the editor’s own line height so the text sits on them. Two palettes ship with it: Notebook Day and Notebook Night. ## What’s done * Sliding sidebar and story river, in sync, in both layout modes and both text directions * Options for full width, the margin rule, the ruled editor, and sticky titles * Not one hardcoded colour. Everything comes from the active palette and is derived with `color-mix()`, so it should re-tint under any palette * Sticky titles that know about the menubar plugin and sit below it instead of under it * Styling for TiddlyDesktop’s wiki list, on desktop and Android * Respects `prefers-reduced-motion`, and the layout stays correct when motion is off * Accessibility. I’ve checked colour contrast, but that’s only part of it. If something looks wrong, please just say what you saw. That has been by far the most useful kind of feedback so far. Thanks for reading.
